title: BoxBoy!
subtitle: A square makes its own tools
summary: BoxBoy! is HAL Laboratory's Nintendo 3DS puzzle platformer about Qbby, a small square who can create connected strings of boxes. Those boxes become bridges, steps, shields or other arrangements for crossing short obstacle courses. The plain monochrome presentation keeps the important relationships visible: the character, the new shape and the space it must occupy. The central ability is deliberately generous in its uses. A small piece of geometry can be detached and moved, or kept attached to Qbby so that the same construction helps his own body reach another place.
body: BoxBoy! is HAL Laboratory's Nintendo 3DS puzzle platformer about Qbby, a small square who can create connected strings of boxes. Those boxes become bridges, steps, shields or other arrangements for crossing short obstacle courses. The plain monochrome presentation keeps the important relationships visible: the character, the new shape and the space it must occupy. The central ability is deliberately generous in its uses. A small piece of geometry can be detached and moved, or kept attached to Qbby so that the same construction helps his own body reach another place.

Each stage limits how many boxes can be produced in a string. Within that allowance, their arrangement determines what can be crossed or blocked. Qbby can push a detached shape into position, while an attached construction can hook a ledge and help pull him upward. Creating a new string removes the previous one, so an arrangement cannot simply accumulate without consequence. The player has to decide which part of a solution is still needed before replacing it. The restriction makes a compact construction meaningful instead of merely increasing the number of pieces.

Groups of stages introduce different hazards and mechanical ideas, such as lasers or cranes. The box-making action remains the reference point, allowing each addition to be understood as another question about the same ability. Nearby checkpoints support experimentation when an arrangement fails. BoxBoy!'s visual restraint is useful here: a solution can look almost obvious once its spatial relationship has been recognised. The pleasure comes from turning an ability described in one sentence into a shape that answers the particular obstacle, then discovering that the next world can ask something different.
